abstract.p: We consider resurgence for the nonconformal Bjorken flow with Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics in the extended relaxation-time approximation. First, we examine the full formal transseries expanded around the equilibrium and then construct the resurgent relation by looking at the structure of Borel-transformed ordinary differential equations. We form a conjecture of the resurgent relation based on the consideration that the Stokes constants constituting the resurgent relation originate only from singularities of dissipative variables on the Borel plane and that the other variables such as temperature and chemical potential become Borel nonsummable through nonlinear terms with the dissipative variables. We numerically check the conjecture for fundamental variables by explicitly evaluating the values of the dominant Stokes constant depending on the initial conditions and the particle mass. We also comment on some issues related to transseries structure and resurgence, such as the case of broken U(1) symmetry, the massless case, generalized relaxation time, and attractor solutions.

sec.label: I.
sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Relativistic hydrodynamics and kinetic theoretical approaches are powerful methods for describing high-energy nuclear collisions theoretically and understanding their nonequilibrium physics based on QCD [1–4]. The Chapman-Enskog (CE) expansion, based on the gradient expansion, encodes the Boltzmann equation into hydrodynamics and has successfully described the nonequilibrium physics of high-energy nuclear collisions in a certain setup called the conformal Bjorken flow, as an IR effective theory [5]. The CE expansion can be regarded as a sort of asymptotic expansion in terms of the Knudsen number around the continuous flow limit determined by Kn≪1. The conformal Bjorken flow, with certain approximations in the collision kernel and its kinetic theoretical approach, can be well formulated by introducing appropriate orthogonal polynomials and a flow time [1–4].

When considering an asymptotic expansion around a near equilibrium by using a certain flow time, dissipative effects, such as shear viscosity, are generally divergent series; i.e., the radius of convergence is zero [5]. In such a case, these asymptotic solutions can be approximations, but there exists a limitation for reducing the error from their exact solution depending on the value of the flow time [5]. However, instead of this disadvantage, this situation implies that a nontrivial relationship between hydro (perturbative) and nonhydro (nonperturbative) modes might be constructable. This relationship can be formulated by employing a mathematical tool called resurgence theory [6,7]. Resurgence theory is a method to extract nonperturbative information from a perturbative expansion (or vice versa) through Borel resummation. These perturbative and nonperturbative sectors can be expressed as transseries, which are a sort of extension of a standard asymptotic expansion by introducing ingredients called transmonomials such as exponential decay and logarithmic convergence, and by using Borel resummation, coefficients in one sector can be expressed by those in the other sectors using singularities on the Borel plane. This relationship is called the resurgent relation [6–13]. In the context of high-energy nuclear collisions, the transseries and resurgence analysis of the conformal Bjorken flow were investigated in Refs. [14–19]. These analyses help us clarify nonperturbative physics out of equilibrium and fundamental questions in hydrodynamics and kinetic theoretical approaches, such as the existence of nonhydro modes and a sort of universality of attractors.

The relevance of the symmetry of a Boltzmann distribution to transseries and its resurgent relation is an interesting question from both physical and mathematical perspectives. Since QCD is not a conformal theory, its nonconformal effects become significant when the temperature is lower relative to particle masses during the time evolution [20,21]. In addition, the nonconformal effects due to particle mass and U(1) (baryon number) become non-negligible at lower energies in the nonequilibrium process of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) [22–24]. Therefore, the assumption of conformal symmetry is broken in the late-time regime of nonequilibrium QCD, and the conformal Bjorken flow needs to be modified to describe such nonequilibrium physics. Transport coefficients and hydrodynamics with/without U(1) symmetry for the nonconformal case have been investigated in Refs. [22–29], and the transseries structure of the nonconformal Bjorken flow without U(1) symmetry changes to extremely nontrivial forms due to the particle mass effect [30].

In this paper, we study the transseries structure and resurgence of the nonconformal Bjorken flow with Fermi-Dirac (FD) and Bose-Enstein (BE) statistics by imposing conservation laws on both the energy-momentum tensor and the current density. We employ the extended relaxation-time approximation to be compatible with microscopic and macroscopic conservation laws [28,31–35]. First, we derive the full formal transseries expanded around the equilibrium. We particularly address the effects of conserved U(1) symmetry and conformal symmetry breaking on the transseries structure. After deriving the formal transseries, we construct the resurgent relation. The main nontrivial points for the construction in our problem are as follows: (i)
Our dynamical system is a multivariable nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) consisting of two types, dYdw=-SY+1w[a+bY]+O(Y2,w-2) and dYdw=Yw[a+bY]+O(Y3w-1,Yw-2), and a variable determined by either type of ODE appears in the other type as (non)linear terms.(ii)
The resurgent relation has a nontrivial dependence on parameters in the theory, such as initial conditions (integration constants) and particle mass.To overcome the above problems, we form a conjecture of the resurgent relation by making observations of the large-order behavior of the perturbative sector and then by focusing on the Borel transformed ODEs.

This paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we briefly review the nonconformal Bjorken flow with FD and BE statistics. In Sec. III, we derive the full formal IR transseries from ODEs. In Sec. IV, we consider the resurgence of the IR transseries. In Sec. V, we make some comments on issues related to transseries and resurgence, such as the case of broken U(1) symmetry, the massless case, generalized relaxation time, and the attractor solution. Section VI is devoted to the summary and discussion. Technical details used in Secs. II–V are summarized in the Appendixes. We take gμν=diag(1,0,0,-τ2) and gμν=diag(1,0,0,-1/τ2) to define the Milne coordinate. We perform the transseries analysis by imposing the Landau frame condition as uνTνμ=Euμ and taking the local rest frame as uμ=(1,0,0,0) in the Milne coordinate. For convenience, we refer to the early-time and late-time regimes as the UV and IR regimes, respectively.

sec.label: II.
sec.title: REVIEW OF NONCONFORMAL BJORKEN FLOW WITH FD AND BE STATISTICS
sec.p: In this section, we briefly review our setup. To avoid complexity, we summarize definitions of symbols used in the below analysis, such as Ξk, Ξk(n), ℵk(n,s), and explicit forms of transport coefficients in Appendix A 1. References [27–29,36] are helpful for the derivation.

We would start with the Boltzmann equation with the relaxation-time approximation. In this work, we employ extended relaxation-time approximation (ERTA) taking the following form [28,31–35]: pμ∂μf(x,p)=C[f],C[f]≔-EpτR(x)[f(x,p)-feq*(x,p)],(1)where f(x,p) is the distribution function, p is the spacial component of the particle momentum pμ satisfying the on-shell condition given by p2=m2, τR is the relaxation-time, and Ep≔u·p is energy on a frame (fluid velocity) uμ. In the ERTA, we introduce feq*(x,p), which is the local equilibrium with thermodynamic frame to be compatible with hydrodynamics and kinetic theory in the collision term. It is defined as feq*(x,p)=1exp[Ep*β*(x)+α*(x)]+a,(2)where β is the inverse temperature and α is defined as α≔μβ using the chemical potential denoted by μ. Additionally, a is a parameter of particle statistics, and taking a=0,+1, and -1 corresponds to Maxwell-Boltzmann (MB), FD, and BE statistics, respectively. Here, the asterisk, *, denotes variables in the thermodynamic frame. These variables (u*μ,β*,α*) include corrections from the gradient expansion and can be decomposed into the zeroth-order part and the correction as O*=O+δO, where δO=O(∂). In this paper, we consider only NS hydro, so we assume that the second- or higher-order corrections in δO is negligible and that (δO)2≈0. We should emphasize that in the ERTA the thermodynamic frame, u*μ, does not need to be the same as uμ, and hydro variables are defined by using uμ, as we will explain later. The latter fluid velocity, uμ, is sometimes called the hydrodynamic frame to distinguish from the thermodynamic frame. Furthermore, on the one hand, (β*,α*) are thermodynamic variables defined in the local equilibrium denoted by feq* on the kinetic theory side, but on the other hand, (β,α) are auxiliary variables constituting hydro variables. Hydro variables can be formally defined by imposing a frame condition (Landau frame in our case) to uμ, and the perfect fluid is defined from the zeroth-order gradient part in feq*, which we denote as feq. See also Refs. [28,31] in detail. From now on, when we say “equilibrium,” we assume that it means hydrodynamic equilibrium, feq.

Before closing the part of transseries construction, we will make comments on the low-temperature (heavy-mass) limit, σβ→+∞. As we can see in Appendix A 3, when taking this limit, the transport coefficients, χβ, and zχβ+χα reduce to functions of only Ra. Since the heavy-mass limit does not change symmetry imposed to the equilibrium, this limit to the formal transseries can be taken without discontinuity happening. However, there exists symmetry emerged by this limit, that is scale invariance in the dynamical system. This heavy-mass limit makes the ODEs given by Eqs. (A110)–(A113) using τR=θ0β to be invariant under the scale transformation defined as (β,Π¯,π¯,R,τ)→(λ-Δββ,λ-ΔΠ¯Π¯,λ-Δπ¯π¯,λ-ΔRR,λτ) with λ∈R, Δβ=-1, and ΔΠ¯=Δπ¯=ΔR=0.5
If one uses α instead of R, D symmetry cannot be seen apparently. This symmetry is called as “D-scale symmetry” in Ref. [30]. The interesting fact in our case is that D-symmetry appears in both the massless and heavy mass limits in contrast to the case of DμNμ≠0 studied in Ref. [30]. When ODEs have D symmetry, one can drop or decouple 1 degree of freedom from the other ODEs by using an appropriate scale-invariant quantity as a flow time. Moreover, since w=θ0τ/τR=τ/β is D-scale invariant, 1/w expansion is essentially the same as the CE expansion in the similar to the conformal Bjorken flow using the same flow time. Indeed, this situation is realized in Eqs. (53) and (60). Oppositely speaking, it can be also said that, for IR transseries of the nonconformal cases, taking care of orders deviating from (θ0/w)k, i.e., aO(s>0)[n,k], is significant to appropriately count contributions from particle kinetic energy.

sec.label: IV.
sec.title: RESURGENCE ANALYSIS
sec.p:
We consider resurgence for the nonconformal Bjorken flow. In Sec. IV A, we first consider the large-order behavior and see Borel summability of fundamental variables in our model, which is helpful to construct the resurgent relation.6
In our paper, the resurgent relation means a relation among coefficients of the PT and NP sectors, that is also called the large-order relation. Then, in Sec. IV B, we construct the resurgent relation. We summarize the review of Borel resummation and the technical details for construction of the resurgent relation in Appendixes B 3 and B 4, respectively. Definitions of symbols related to Borel resummation are also summarized in Appendix B 3. For technical simplicity, we use T=1/β defined as T∼σβ-1w-2∑n∈N02∑k∈N0aT[n,k]ζnw-k,(69)in place of β.7
One can perform the same analysis described below by using β.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: Large-order behavior
sec.p: Before considering resurgence, we first see the large-order behavior of the PT sector and remind the reader how it relates to the first NP sector. In our analysis, instead of dealing with (Π¯,π¯), we consider X˜± defined as (X˜+,X˜-)⊤=U(Π¯,π¯)⊤, where U is a constant matrix given by Eq. (B7). It is because the linearized equation of X˜± gives the NP transmonomials, ζ±, as two independent solutions, so it can be expected that a relation of the large-order behavior of the PT sector to the NP sector can be more clearly seen than keeping (Π¯,π¯). Additionally, as we saw in Sec. III, the coefficients are polynomials of (σβθ02)-1. For now, we expand the coefficients with respect to (σβθ02)-1 such as Eq. (50) and consider the spanned formal series expansion labeled by a fixed order of (σβθ02)-1 defined as X˜±(s)≔∑k∈N0aX˜±(s)[0,k][σR,a,θ0]w-k.(70)Thus, X˜±=∑s∈N0X˜±(s)(σβθ02)-s. It is notable that, since X˜± is a dimensionless variable, the particle mass appears as coupling only to σβ in the transseries when explicitly turning on m. In this sense, it would be worth it to take the form (70) to consider the mass dependence in the resurgent relation. We write down the form of transseries of X˜± in Appendix B 2 a.

Let us first remember the relation between the large-order behavior of the PT sector and the first NP sector by taking the following ansatz to the large kth order of aX˜±(s)[0,k]: aX˜±(s)[0,k+1]aX˜±(s)[0,k]≃b±(s)k+c±(s)(k≫1),(71)where b±(s)∈R+ and c±(s)∈R. The positive b±(s) guarantees a positive or negative series, which means that X˜±(s) is Borel nonsummable. If this ansatz really works, then a coefficient of the higher order can be approximated as aX˜±(s)[0,k]≃M±(s)b±(s)k-1(c±(s)/b±(s)+1)k-1(k≫1)=M±(s)b±(s)k-1Γ(k+c±(s)/b±(s))Γ(1+c±(s)/b±(s))(72)with M±(s)∈R, where (a)n is the Pochhammer symbol. Since acting the Borel transform to X˜±(s) yields B[X˜±(s)]=∑k∈NaX˜±(s)[0,k]Γ(k)ξk-1≃M±(s)(1-b±(s)ξ)c±(s)/b±(s)+1(k≫1),(73)the leading order of discontinuity on the real positive axis on the Borel plane is found as (S0+-S0-)[X˜±(s)]∝∼e-w/b±(s)w-c±(s)/b±(s)(k≫1).(74)Equation (74) means that the large-order behavior (71) directly relates to the transmonomial in the NP sector and suggests that the b±(s) and c±(s) can be expressed by using S and ρ± given by Eq. (29).

The question is if one can extract a value of (b±(s),c±(s)), which is consistent with the result of NP sectors from coefficients of the PT sector. To see it, we plot the ratio of the coefficients given in Eq. (71) for s=0,…,5 evaluated from the MB statistics (a=0) in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b). One can observe that X˜±(s) is in general an alternating series in the lower order of k because the ratio is negative, but it becomes a positive or negative series in the higher order. We also estimate (b±(s),c±(s)) for the asymptotic lines from these plots, and the results are consistent with that b±(s)=1/S=θ0/3, c+(s)=-ρ+/S≈3.390·θ0, and c-(s)=-(ρ++2)/S≈2.723·θ0 for any s∈N0. We also plot the same quantity of (T,R) in Figs. 3(c) and 3(d). One can observe that they have the behavior similar to X˜±, i.e., divergent series and Borel nonsummable. The numerical fitting using the same function to Eq. (71) shows that bT,R(s)=1/S, cT(s)=-(ρ++3)/S≈2.390·θ0, and cR(s)=-(ρ++1)/S≈3.057·θ0. In summary, we found the following observations: (I)
According to Eqs. (B10) and (B11), the lowest order of (σβθ02)-1 in the NP sectors depends on the order of w-1. However, the fitting result using Eq. (71) is independent on s.(II)
The ratios of coefficients of all of (T,R,X˜±) have large-order behaviors similar to each other, such as exactly the same gradient, roughly the same intercept, and being Borel nonsummable.(III)
c-(s) seems to be irrelevant to the value of ρ- or extremely far from it.Observation III can be easily solved by looking to the dominant part of X˜-np. According to Eq. (B11) and the value of ρ± in Eq. (29), the lowest order of X˜-np is proportional to ζ+/w2, and thus, (ρ++2) in the result of c-(s) comes from this exponent of w.

sec.p: The observations I and II are more nontrivial and should be closely related to structure of the ODEs determining the resurgent structure. As we can see later, however, both of them can be actually solved by focusing on the Borel transformed ODEs and introducing Stokes constants appropriately. We will discuss these issues in detail in Sec. IV B.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: Construction of the resurgent relation
sec.p:
In this section, we construct the resurgent relation, i.e., the large-order relation. In general, the form of resurgent relation is closely related to forms of given ODEs and structure of the Borel plane of Borel transformed variables. We normally employ some methods such as the Padá approximant to predict the resurgent structure, but those methods are not always helpful for the structure when a given problem is not so simple, e.g., multivariable ODEs consisting of different types.8
In general, the existence of singularities on the real positive axis in the Borel plane is not a sufficient condition to say that the theory contains nonperturbative effects. In such a case, Borel resummed functions (or transseries) obtained by S0± include nonperturbative effects, but the effects vanish by eliminating discontinuity using the median resummation, Smed≔S0+∘S−1/2=S0−∘S+1/2. This special situation can be indeed observed in a quantum mechanics. See Ref. [39], for example.Roughly, our problem consists of two types of ODEs: dYdw=-SY+1w[a+bY]+O(Y2,w-2) and dYdw=Yw[a+bY]+O(Y3w-1,Yw-2). For this reason, in our analysis, we will take the following procedure: (1) identifying the number of Stokes constants by looking to the Borel transformed ODEs, (2) forming a conjecture of the resurgent relation which is consistent with the observations I and II in Sec. IV A, and (3) numerically checking the resurgent relation.

First, we consider the Borel transformed ODEs. We define the Borel transform as OB≔B[O]. Action of it to the ODEs (20)–(23) yields9
In these equations, we used the simplified notation for the Landau symbol O(•) to omit the convolution with RB, such that O(RB*n*OB)→O(OB), because RB=σR·id+O(Iξ) and the order of ξ in O^ does not change by the convolution with RB. -ξTB=-2Iξ*TB*[id+O(TB,X˜±B)],(75)-ξRB=-18Iξ*RB*[(id+a22RB)*{(31-1285)X˜+B+(31+1285)X˜-B}+O(TB,X˜±B*2)],(76)-ξX˜±B=-SX˜±B+Iξ*[43(1∓1285257)·id+O(TB,X˜±B)]+O(TB,X˜±B*2),(77)where B[dOdw]=-ξOB, Iξ≔B[w-1], * denotes the convolution defined as fB*gB(ξ)≔∫0ξdξ′fB(ξ′)gB(ξ-ξ′), and OB*2≔OB*OB. In addition, “id” is the identity operator under the convolution,10
This identity operator is defined as id≔B[1] and has a different sense from the symbol, Iξ≔B[w-1]. Thus, if Y(w)=∑k∈N0aY[k]w-k, then its Borel transformation is expressed as B[Y](ξ)=aY[0]·id+aY[1]Iξ+∑k∈N+1aY[k]Γ(k)ξk-1. i.e., id*OB=OB*id=OB. The Borel transformed ODEs (75)–(77) tell us several pieces of information about the mechanism of the resurgence of our ODEs. First, X˜±B has a singularity at ξ=S. This fact can be easily seen from Eq. (77) by making the form to be X˜±B=(S-ξ)-1·[⋯]. Because of the singularity in X˜±B, quadratic terms of X˜±B generate a new singularity at ξ=2S.11
Intuitively, it can be found in the following way. Consider fB(ξ)=ξsS-ξ and gB(ξ)=ξtS-ξ with s,t∈N0. Then, fB*gB=h(ξ)log(1-ξ/S)2S-ξ+(reg.) with a regular function h(ξ) depending on s, t at ξ=2S. Thus, a new singularity appears at ξ=2S. By repeating the similar computation, one can find that singularities exist at ξ=nS with n∈N. Second, the PF sector of (T,R) is Borel summable (convergent series). It can be shown from Eqs. (75) and (76) by setting X˜±B=0 and considering if all terms contain the same type of singularities such as the location and the order.12
One can find the observation in the following way. Equation (75) can be written by TB=2ξ-1Iξ*TB*[id+O(TB)]. Assume that TB has a term such as ξ(1-ξ/A)-c with real positive constants, A and c, and that it does not have another type of singularities. By easy computations, one can find the fact that ξ-1Iξ*TB generates the log singularity at ξ=A, which contradicts to our assumption. The regularity of RB can be shown in a similar way. Third, for a similar reason as that of the first, i.e., because of nonlinear terms with X˜±B, singularities of (TB,RB) appear at the same locations, ξ=nS with n∈N. In summary, these considerations imply that the origin of Borel nonsummable for (T,R,X˜±) comes from the singularities only in X˜±B and that (T,R) becomes Borel nonsummable indirectly through nonlinear terms with X˜±.

If this is the case, it means that the resurgence of X˜± is essentially the same as that of dYdw=-ΛY-1w[V+BY]+O(Y2,w-2),(78)where V is a constant vector and Λ and B are constant diagonal matrices. The resurgence of this type of ODE has been known, for example, in Refs. [12,15–17], and the cancellation of discontinuity in the resulting Borel resummed function (or transseries) is obtained by introducing two Stokes constants as S0+[X˜±(w;σ-12A)]=S0-[X˜±(w;σ+12A)],(79)where σ=(σ+,σ-)∈R2 and A=(A+,A-)∈(iR)2 are vectorial forms of the integration constants and the Stokes constants, respectively. Furthermore, by using this formula, the resurgent relation among the PT and NP sectors is obtained as aX˜±[0,k]≃12πi∑(n+,n-)∈N02|n|>0∑h∈N0A+n+A-n-C(|n|,n-)aX˜±[n,h]Γ(k-n·ρ-h)(n·S)k-n·ρ-h(k≫1),(80)where C(p,q)=(pq) is the binomial coefficient and n=(n+,n-). In addition, S=(S+,S-) and ρ=(ρ+,ρ-) are defined by Eq. (29). The derivation is summarized in Appendix B 4. If we take the form similar to Eq. (78) for X˜±, then the constant parts should have the dependence of the integration constants, (σβ,σR), which also means that the Stokes constants have similar dependence. From the fact that the coefficients of transseries are polynomials expanded by (σβθ02)-1, we put the ansatz to the Stokes constants such that A±[σβ,σR,a,θ0]=∑s∈N0A±(s)[σR,a,θ0](σβθ02)-s(A±[σR,a,θ0]∈iR).Notice that this ansatz takes care of observation I in Sec. IV A by supposing that the contribution from A±(s=0) is more dominant than A±(s>0).

It is straightforward to construct the resurgent relation of (T,R) by using the facts that no singularity appears in their Borel transformed ODEs with X˜±B=0 and that the Borel resummation is homomorphism, i.e., Sθ[f·g]=Sθ[f]·Sθ[g]. Since the cancellation of discontinuity (79) can be obtained by the shift of the integration constants which gives solutions of the same ODEs, the same equality should be satisfied for the r.h.s. of the ODEs, i.e., S0+[FO](w;σ-12A)=S0-[FO](w;σ+12A), where O∈{T,R} and FT,R are defined in Eqs. (20) and (21),13
FT is defined from Fβ as FT≔-T2Fβ. which eventually gives S0+[O](w;σ-12A)=S0-[O](w;σ+12A) for O∈{T,R}. Therefore, the resurgent relation for (T,R) has to be the same form as Eq. (80). It is notable that this consideration is also extendable to variables which are functions of (T,R,X˜±) using the property of homomorphism of the Borel resummation, i.e., Sθ[O(T,R,X˜±)]=O(Sθ[T],Sθ[R],Sθ[X˜±]).(81)In addition, the σR,a dependence in the Stokes constants are given by the functional form of the transport coefficients. Since in practice it is extremely hard to obtain their precise forms expanded around β=+∞ for all orders, we would assume that they are analytic functions in a neighborhood of R=0.

Let us form a conjecture by summarizing the above considerations. We form the following conjecture of the resurgent relation which is consistent with the observations I and II in Sec. IV A. Conjecture.
Suppose that O is a function of (T,R,X˜±) and its transseries expanded around the equilibrium takes the form O(w)∼Bwp∑k∈N0aO[n,k]ζnw-kas w→+∞(B,p∈R),(82)where B and p are determined by the functional form of O. Then, O satisfies the resurgent relation given by aO[0,k]≃12πi∑(n+,n-)∈N02|n|>0∑h∈N0A+n+A-n-C(|n|,n-)aO[n,h]Γ(k-n·ρ-h)(n·S)k-n·ρ-h(k≫1),(83)where A± is the Stokes constant taking the form A±[σβ,σR,a,θ0]=∑s∈N0A±(s)[σR,a,θ0](σβθ02)-s(A±[σR,a,θ0]∈iR)(84)and A±(s)[σR,a,θ0] is an analytic function in a neighborhood of σR,a=0 for any s∈N0.

The essential point of this conjecture is that, because of the dependence of the integration constants, (σβ,σR,a), in the transseries of O, the Stokes constant, A±, is not just a constant but an analytic function of (σβ,σR,a), i.e., Taylor expandable around (σβ,σR,a)=(+∞,0). Equation (84) is the expanded form in terms only of (σβθ02)-1 in accordance with analysis in Sec. IV A. The similar analysis in the case of A±=const. has been studied, e.g., in Refs. [9,11], so our conjecture is a sort of generalization from the case. Notice that Eq. (83) contains the contributions of all the branch cuts, originated from the NP sectors labeled by (n+,n-), along the positive real axis on the Borel plane.

Since the Stokes constants are analytic functions, the resurgent relation (83) can take a slightly different form by expanding σβ and σR,a. For simplicity, let us consider the case that O∈{β,R,X˜±}. Substituting Eqs. (50), (59), and (84) into Eq. (83) yields the resurgent relation for a fixed s as aO(s)[0,k]≃12πi∑n∈N02|n|>0∑m∈N02∑h∈N0A+(m+)n+A-(m-)n-C(|n|,n-)aO(s-n·m)[n,h]⁢Γ(k-n·ρ-h)(n·S)k-n·ρ-h,(85)where aO(t<0)[n,h]=0. Additionally, the expanded form by both σβ and σR,a can be obtained by expanding the components in the resurgent relation as aO(s)[n,k]=∑t∈N0aO(s,t)[n,k](σR,a)t, A±(s)=∑t∈N0A±(s,t)(σR,a)t, and ρ±=∑t∈N0ρ±(t)(σR,a)t. The results for t=0, 1 are expressed by aO(s,0)[0,k]≃12πi∑n∈N02|n|>0∑m∈N02∑h∈N0A+(m+,0)n+A-(m-,0)n-C(|n|,n-)aO(s-n·m,0)[n,h]⁢Γ(k-n·ρ(0)-h)(n·S)k-n·ρ(0)-h,(86)aO(s,1)[0,k]≃12πi∑n∈N02|n|>0∑m∈N02∑h∈N0A+(m+,0)n+A-(m-,0)n-C(|n|,n-)⁢aO(s-n·m,0)[n,h]Γ(k-n·ρ(0)-h)(n·S)k-n·ρ(0)-h·[n+A+(m+,1)A+(m+,0)+n-A-(m-,1)A-(m-,0)+aO(s-n·m,1)[n,h]aO(s-n·m,0)[n,h]+(log(n·S)-ψ(0)(k-n·ρ0-h))n·ρ(1)](ρ±(1)=3/2),(87)where ψ(0)(x) is the polygamma function.14
log(n·S) and ψ(0)(k-n·ρ0-h) in Eq. (86) imply that another type of transmonomials, logw, appears due to expanding the higher transmonomial, ζ±, by σR,a [13]. It can be seen as ζ±=e-S±wwρ±=e-S±wwρ±(0)∑n∈N0(-δρ±logw)nn!, where δρ±≔ρ±-ρ±(0) is the σR,a-dependent part in ρ±. Notice that S± is independent on σR,a. It is notable that the mass dependence is also contained in Eq. (83) by turning on m as σβ→mσβ.

Finally, we numerically check the above conjecture. Because of the property of homomorphism of the Borel resummation (81), it is enough to check the conjecture for (T,R,X˜±) only. Since the essential point of our conjecture is that the Stokes constants are analytic functions, we employ Eqs. (86) and (87), which are constructed by fully using the analyticity. These indicate that the resurgent relation individually holds for each the fixed s and t in aO(s,t)[0,k]. For the numerical check, one first has to determine the value of the Stokes constants. The values of them depend on the normalization of σ±, so we take aX˜+[(1,0),0]=aX˜-[(0,1),0]=1.15
This normalization is the same choice taken in Eqs. (55)–(58). According to Eq. sec.label: V.
sec.title: ADDITIONAL REMARKS
sec.p: Our results have relations to various topics related to hydrodynamization of heavy-ion collisions and its resurgence. In this section, we make comments on some issues related to the transseries structure and the resurgence of the nonconformal Bjorken flow with FD and BE statics. In Sec. V A, we describe the case of broken U(1) symmetry and the difference of the transseries. In Sec. V B, we consider the transseries structure and the resurgence under the massless limit. In Sec. V C, we briefly describe the transseries structure in the case of the generalized relaxation time. In Sec. V D, we discuss attractor solutions from the aspect of the IR transseries.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: Case of broken U(1) symmetry
sec.p: For comparison with our result, we briefly describe the case of broken U(1) symmetry. Since imposing U(1) symmetry as DμNμ=0 determines dynamics of the chemical potential, one can take μ=α=0 when DμNμ≠0. In such a case, Eq. (A44) gives -Dβ·Ξ3(1)+(E+P+Π)θ-πμνσμν=0⇒Dβ≈βχβθ,(88)and the speed of sound (cs2=χβ) is given by [26] χβ=β-1(E0+P)Ξ1(1)Ξ3(1)∼z-1-12z-2+O(z-3)+ae-z22(z-1-5116z-2+O(z-3))+O(e-2z)as z→+∞.(89)The crucial point is that the leading order of χβ is O(z-1) in spite of O(z0) in the case of conserved U(1) symmetry. This difference makes a drastic change to the transseries structure. The PF sector under the Bjorken symmetry is easily obtained from the expanded form of cs2 as βpf∼logτ[1-log(2)τ2logτ+σβlogτ+O((logτ)-2)-ae-σβ22·1τ(logτ)1/2(1-4316logτ+O((logτ)-2))+O(τ-2)],(90)where log(2)τ≔loglogτ, and we took m=1 in this expression. The set of transmonomials constructing the PF sector is {(logτ)-1,log(2)τ} for the MB statistics (a=0) and {τ-1,(logτ)-1/2,log(2)τ} for the FD and BE statistics (a=±1). Apparently, this structure is totally different from the case of conserved U(1) symmetry. Since the structure of PF sector propagates to the PT and NP sectors, the whole structure of transseries entirely changes. Transseries analysis for the MB statistics has been studied in Ref. [30]. The a dependence is beginning with O(τ-1) in βpf and becomes negligible near the equilibrium. The translation between τ and w can be performed by Eq. (26), and the leading order is obtained as w∼τ(logτ)-1 or τ∼wlogw. Hence, the transseries structure of w is essentially the same as that of τ.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: Massless case
sec.p: We make comments on the massless case. The crucial point is that, since the massless limit is not commutative with the asymptotic limit, w→+∞, transseries in the massless theory cannot be directly found from Eq. (28) by taking the massless limit. Conversely, this implies the fact that, as is also seen in Sec. V A, transseries structure is generally determined by symmetry of the equilibrium point and works as far as the symmetry is not enhanced or broken by taking certain parameters in the theory.

Here, let us briefly see transseries and resurgence by beginning with the massless ODEs. As is described in Appendix A 4, the massless ODEs using τR=βθ0 and w=τ/β are given by dβdw=βw·13-π¯23+π¯,dRdw=-3Rw·Li3(Ra)Li2(Ra)·π¯23+π¯,dπ¯dw=-π¯θ0+1w[-43β¯π(Ra)+3821π¯+D(Ra)π¯2]23+π¯,(91)where β¯π(Ra)≔415·Li2(Ra)Li4(Ra)4Li2(Ra)Li4(Ra)-3Li3(Ra)2,D(Ra)≔4-3Li3(Ra)2(3Li1(Ra)Li3(Ra)-2Li2(Ra)2)Li2(Ra)2(4Li2(Ra)Li4(Ra)-3Li3(Ra)2),with R≔e-α and Ra≔-aR. Notice that the ODE of α is defined as dαdw=3w·Li3(Ra)Li2(Ra)·π¯23+π¯.(92)One can immediately see that the β dependence does not exist in the ODEs of R and π¯. From these ODEs, the PF sector is obtained by taking π¯=0, and thus, βpf∼σβw1/2,Rpf∼σR,αpf∼-logσR(w≫1),(93)where σβ∈R+ and σR∈R+ are integration constants. Because w∼(σβ-1τ)2/3, the large-order behavior of βpf is βpf∼σβ2/3τ-1/3. The leading order of the chemical potential, μ=α/β, is given by μpf=αpf/βpf∼-σβ-1logσR·w-1/2, and thus, limw→+∞μpf=0.

The IR transseries essentially has the same form as that of the massive case but contains different values of S and ρ, β∼σβw1/2∑n∈N0∑k∈N0aβ[n,k]ζnw-k,R∼σR∑n∈N0∑k∈N0aR[n,k]ζnw-k,π¯∼∑n∈N0∑k∈N0aπ¯[n,k]ζnw-k,(94)where ζ≔σπ¯e-Swwρ,S≔32θ0,ρ≔197+3β¯π(σR,a),(95)with σR,a≔-aσR. The normalization of the integration constants can be fixed by taking aβ[0,0]=aR[0,0]=aπ¯[1,0]=1 without the loss of generality. The leading order of π¯ can be directly computed as π¯∼43β¯π(σR,a)·θ0was w→+∞,(96)so all of the coefficients, (aβ[n,k],aR[n,k],aπ¯[n,k]), are functions of σR,a. In addition, aO[n,k]∝θ0k due to lack of the σβ dependence in R and π¯.

In the similar way as in the nonconformal case, the resurgent relation is obtained as aπ¯[0,k]≃12πi∑n∈N∑h∈N0Anaπ¯[n,h]Γ(k-nρ-h)(nS)k-nρ-h(k≫1),(97)where A∈iR is the Stokes constant. The coefficients, aπ¯[n,k], and ρ can be expanded in terms of σR,a, so the Stokes constant also depends on σR,a. Not only π¯ but also (β,R) are Borel nonsummable divergent series because of nonlinear terms with π¯ in the ODEs. In addition, the same resurgent relation (97) is satisfied for (β,R).

We would like to emphasize that, as well as the massive case, the IR transseries cannot be continuously connected to that of broken U(1) symmetry, DμNμ≠0. Naively thinking, it looks like transseries of broken U(1) symmetry can be realized by taking a certain limit to parameters. However, although transmonomials between the two cases are the same, this expectation is not correct. The easiest way to see this fact is making sure if σR can be taken as a value corresponding to μ=0, i.e., R=1, for any w. But from the ODE of R in Eq. (95), one can immediately see that R≠1 because π¯∼O(w-1) and is nonzero. Another way is evaluating UV convergent points to which flows converge in the UV limit, w→0+. Indeed, the values between the cases with and without U(1) symmetry are different from each other. It is because, when deriving the ODEs with DμNμ=0, contribution from the chemical potential has to be taken into account under the assumption that dαdτ≠0. Therefore, the ODE of π¯ originally does not match with the one without U(1) symmetry.

sec.label: C.
sec.title: Generalized relaxation time: τR(x,p)=(βEp)γtR(x)
sec.p: We make comments on the transseries structure for the generalized relaxation time. One can generalize the relaxation time to depend on the momentum p, for example, as [28,40–44] τR(x,p)=(βEp)γtR(x)(γ∈R),(98)where tR(x) is a relaxation time depending only on x.

The important fact for transseries is that the PF sector does not change at all. It is because the PF sector is irrelevant to the collision part. Thus, the large-order behavior of the PF sector is also the same as βpf∼σβ(mτ)2/3 and αpf∼-σβ(mτ)2/3. When computing the PT sector, the effect of γ needs to be taken care of. If τR is given as Eq. (98), then the collision part in the ODEs replaced such as X¯τR→X¯τR,X¯=X¯tRzγ(1+O(z-1))(X¯∈{Π¯,π¯}),(99)where τR,X¯∼tRzγ(1+O(z-1)) is the effective relaxation time associated with Π¯ or π¯, and z≔mβ. In contrast, the noncollision part is essentially the same form as [C0β¯Π,π(Ra)+O(z-1,Π¯,π¯)]/τ, where C0β¯Π,π(Ra) denotes the O(z0) part of β¯Π,π depending on γ. Notice that the explicit form of transport coefficients depends on γ, but only the coefficients change when taking the asymptotic expansion around z=+∞. It is because Ξk and Ξk(n) are O(z-3/2) for any n∈N and k∈R.

The convergence to the equilibrium is naturally obtained under the assumption that the collision part is dominant relative to the noncollision part around the equilibrium, so it gives a constraint to the value of γ depending on the definition of tR. Here, we suppose that tR∝∼τδ with δ∈R around the equilibrium. One can obtain the constraint as 1tRzγ∝∼τ-(δ+23γ)≫τ-1as τ→+∞⇒γ<32(1-δ).(100)Notice that taking tR=βθ0 gives γ<1/2. The asymptotics of (Π¯,π¯) also depends on γ, and the leading order is given by Π¯∼O(τ2(δ+23γ-1)),π¯∼O(τδ+23γ-1).(101)

When thinking of transseries analysis including the PT and NP sectors, the choice of the flow time w might be crucial. In this case, there is no flow time to make the collision part as const.×X¯ for both Π¯ and π¯ simultaneously, but the definition of w that we used in the above analysis essentially works for construction of transseries. Let us see this fact by taking tR=βθ0 (δ=2/3) and the flow time as w=τ(βzγ)-1. Below, we take the mass unit, m=1. Since the derivative for the variable transformation is given by dwdτ=1-(1+γ)(χβ+Π¯-π¯)β1+γ,(102)the ODEs take the form as dΠ¯dw=-31-2γ[Π¯θ0+1w{C0β¯Π(Ra)+O(β-1,X¯)}]+O(β-1X¯,X¯2),(103)dπ¯dw=-31-2γ[π¯θ0+1w{-43C0β¯π(Ra)+O(β-1,X¯)}]+O(β-1X¯,X¯2).(104)From these ODEs, the leading orders of variables are expressed as βpf∼σβw2/(1-2γ), αpf∼-σβw2/(1-2γ), Π¯∼aΠ¯[σR,a](θ0w)2, and π¯∼aπ¯[σR,a]θ0w, where aΠ¯,π¯[σR,a] is a function of σR,a depending on γ. In addition, if the exponent of the exponential decay in the NP transmonomial is proportional to w such as e-Sw, then it gives another constraint to γ, that comes from O(β-1X¯) in the ODEs16
If γ<-1/2, then the exponential decay is exp[-3(1-2γ)θ0w-S1w-1+2γ1-2γ] with a real constant S1.: limw→+∞∫dwβpf=0orO(logw)⇒γ≥-12.(105)Hence, when γ is in the range -1/2≤γ<1/2, the transseries can be obtained as the form similar to Eq. (28) but with different S± and ρ±. The transmonomial generating the power expansion is relevant to cardinality of γ, i.e., γ∈Q or γ∈R\Q [12,45]. The PT sector is a single expansion generated by {w-1/q} with q=lcm(1-2γ,2)/2∈N if γ∈Q but a double expansion by {w-1,w-2/(1-2γ)} otherwise. Therefore, the transseries are given by β∼w2/(1-2γ)σβ∑n∈N02∑k∈N0aβ[n,k]ζnw-k/q,R∼σR∑n∈N02∑k∈N0aR[n,k]ζnw-k/q,X¯∼∑n∈N02∑k∈N0aX¯[n,k]ζnw-k/q(X¯∈{Π¯,π¯})(106)for γ∈Q or β∼w2/(1-2γ)σβ∑n∈N02∑k∈N02aβ[n,k]ζnw-k1-2k2/(1-2γ),R∼σR∑n∈N02∑k∈N02aR[n,k]ζnw-k1-2k2/(1-2γ),X¯∼∑n∈N02∑k∈N02aX¯[n,k]ζnw-k1-2k2/(1-2γ)(X¯∈{Π¯,π¯})(107)otherwise.

It is possible to construct the resurgent relation with γ∈Q in the similar way described in Appendix B 4, and one can obtain it as the same form as our conjecture. In contrast, for the resurgent relation with γ∈R\Q, one has to take care of branch cuts caused by the fractional power in the double expansion, and the form of the relation should be more nontrivial. This construction is beyond the scopes of our main purpose, so we do not argue this issue in this paper.

sec.label: D.
sec.title: Attractor solution from the aspect of IR transseries
sec.p: We consider the attractor solution from the aspect of IR transseries. An attractor is known as an invariant subspace of flow (ISOF) defined on the flow subspace of dissipative hydro variables to which flows deviating from the ISOF converge. A convergent rate to the attractor is expected as a key point of universality characterizing a given system and for the memory-loss effect of the UV domain. Those attractors have been well studied in both the conformal and nonconformal systems, e.g., in Refs. [3,14,15,30,46–56].

When considering a nonautonomous system, it is convenient to prepare a trivial bundle defined as M=F×T, where the fiber is a space of the dynamical variables, i.e., (β,R,Π¯,π¯)∈F=R+2×R2, and the base space is defined as a space of the flow time, w∈T=R≥0 [57,58].17
Since our ODEs are a nonautonomous system, the shift symmetry of a flow time as w→w0 is broken. In such a case, flow has to be defined on a tangent space including the time axis. In high-energy nuclear collision hydro physics, people normally look at its projected subspace spanned by viscous variables and a flow time, i.e., M^=F^×T, where (Π¯,π¯)∈F^=R2, and investigate existence of an attractor and its property. On this projected subspace, at least in the conformal case, an attractor solution is considered as a one-dimensional invariant subspace of flows, but in the nonconformal case, this aspect is not always correct in the sense that the initial condition of (β,R) changes the flow structure on M^. This means that (β0,R0)≔(β(w0),R(w0)) at a fixed w0 are control parameters of flows on M^, and an attractor (in the physical sense) is defined as a three-dimensional invariant subspace of flows embedded on the original total space, M. In contrast, the conformal case without U(1) symmetry is special. In this case, the attractor is originally a two-dimensional invariant subspace of flows on the total space defined as M=F×T with (β,π¯)∈F=R+×R and w∈T=R≥0, but when using w=τ/τR, it is enough to look at its projected subspace M^=F^×T with π¯∈F^ for seeing flows of π¯ because the dynamics of β is decoupled in the ODE of π¯ due to the existence of D symmetry [30]. Therefore, the conformal attractor without U(1) symmetry can be projected onto M^ without missing its information and regarded as a one-dimensional object on M^. However, in the nonconformal case, even if U(1) symmetry is not imposed, this logic does not work in general.

One can investigate convergent rates of the attractor in the IR regime, i.e., (local) forward attractor, by using the IR transseries (28) and considering perturbation from the attractor.18
We consider only the IR regime. So, we suppose that this attractor is a local forward attractor but do not need to impose the conditions of pullback attractor for this discussion [57,58]. As we consider in Appendix C, any convergent points do not appear in the UV limit when using w for the flow time. Suppose that we prepared Y0≔(β0,R0)=(β(w0),R(w0)) at a fixed time, w=w0. Then, an attractor can be found by tuning the initial condition of X¯=(Π¯,π¯) and solving the ODEs, which we denote as X¯att(w;Y0). If one slightly perturbs X¯ from X¯att at w=w0 as X¯(w0;Y0)=X¯att(w0;Y0)+δX¯(w0;Y0), it corresponds to perturbation of the integration constants in the IR transseries. The point is that the perturbation of two variables possibly changes all of the integration constants as (σβ,att+δσβ,σR,att+δσR,σ±,att+δσ±), where σO,att≔σO(Y0,X¯att(w0;Y0)), because the initial condition at a fixed time relates to the integration constants through a nontrivial relationship. Thus, for w≫1, one can easily compute the perturbation as δβ∼δσβw2,δR∼δσR,δΠ¯∼0.5500·aδσRθ02w-2+(9.3333+aσR,att)·δσβσβ,att2θ02w-4-0.8569·δσ+e-S+wwρ+(0),δπ¯∼0.2357·aδσRθ0w-1+(3.1111+aσR,att)·δσβσβ,att2θ0w-3+1.0000·δσ+e-S+wwρ+(0),(108)where ρ±(0) is the zeroth order of ρ± expanded around σR,a=0. Here, we omitted the contribution from δσ- because the effect of δσ+ is generally more dominant. Notice that w∼(σβ,att-1τ)1/3 in the nonconformal case. The result implies that the convergent rate near the equilibrium is a power law because of the existence of chemical potential and/or particle mass. The exponential decay coupling to δσ+ is expected to be relevant to a single-line effect and memory-loss of initial conditions. To see the effect, one has to choose an initial condition such that |aδσR|≪1 and |δσβ/σβ,att2|≪1. When taking the MB statistics (a=0), the first condition is trivially satisfied. One can satisfy the second condition by taking a sufficiently large σβ,att, i.e., setting a sufficiently small temperature in the initial condition compared with the mass unit.

The above consideration based on asymptotic analysis tells us that special behaviors such as a single line effect and globally defined “universality” generally do not exist in the nonconformal Bjorken flow. It is because the perturbation from the attractor holds various decay rates even just around the equilibrium and extracting a certain decay rate from them is essentially a fine-tuning problem of the initial condition. This statement is unchanged for any variable which is a function of (β,R,Π¯,π¯). It is also important to note that, in a nonautonomous system, changing only w0 as fixing values of the initial condition changes the flow structure on M^ because Y0 has the same value but is given at a different w0.

The massless case can be also obtained by using Eq. (95). In a similar way, one can find δβ∼δσβw1/2,δR∼δσR,δπ¯∼0.0667·aδσRθ0w-1+δσπ¯e-Swwρ(0).(109)In the massless case, the leading order of w in terms of τ is written as w∼(σβ,att-1τ)2/3. When taking the FD or BE statistics, i.e., a=±1, the change of initial condition affects σR, so it gives a power law. In the MB case (a=0), in contrast, the leading order is exponential decay, which is thought to be related to a single-line effect.

sec.label: VI.
sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: In this paper, we have considered transseries analysis and resurgence of the nonconformal Bjorken flow with Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics on the relaxation-time approximation by imposing conservation laws to both the energy-momentum tensor and the current density.

We have first obtained the full formal transseries expanded around the equilibrium using the flow time defined as w=τ/β in Sec. III. The conservation law of current density drastically changes the physics around equilibrium in the nonconformal case. The effect of U(1) symmetry enters not only into the transport coefficients but also into the speed of sound which determines the explicit form of the transmonomials in the transseries. In our setup, the large-order behavior of (β,α,Π¯,π¯) around the equilibrium is a power law with respect to w=τ/β(∼τ1/3). In particular, the temperature behaves as β∼w2∼τ2/3, and the value of exponent correctly deviates from 1/3, which is the feature of the conformal symmetry breaking. This statement is also true for the Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics that the chemical potential is decoupled in the ODEs of viscosities (Π¯,π¯). The PT sector is a formal power expansion, and the NP sectors include exponential decay as e-n·Sw/wn·ρ. The coefficients in all the sectors depend on the integration constants (σβ,σR), and the particle mass appears only as coupling with σβ as mσβ. The transseries structure is sensitive to symmetry of the equilibrium, and emerging/breaking symmetry causes a drastic change to the structure. These IR transseries derived from the equilibrium imposed different symmetry, i.e., with/without a particle mass and/or U(1) symmetry, are not continuously connected to each other even by taking the limit for parameters in the theories.

We have considered the resurgence by forming a conjecture of the resurgent relation structure of the Borel transformed ODEs in Sec. IV. Whereas the Borel transformed ODEs of (Π¯,π¯) (or X˜±) explicitly contain singularities on the positive real axis of the Borel plane, discontinuity of (T,R) by Borel resummation is indirectly caused by nonlinear terms with (Π¯,π¯) in the ODEs of them. As a result, the PF sector which is Borel summable becomes Borel nonsummable in the PT sector. This situation affects the number of Stokes constants in the resurgent relation, i.e., the resurgent relation needs two Stokes constants associated with (Π¯,π¯) that depend on the initial conditions and the particle mass. We have numerically checked that all of (T,R,X˜±) satisfy the conjectured resurgent relation provided in Eq. (83) by explicitly evaluating the value of the dominant Stokes constant. We summarized the transseries structure and the resurgence in Fig. 4.

caption.p: Schematic figure of transseries structure and resurgence. The transseries structure is beginning with the speed of sound, cs2, that determines the PF sector. By using the result of the PF sector, the leading order of (Π¯pt,π¯pt) is obtained, and then, all coefficients of the PT sector can be recursively computed order by order. The PT sector is a formal power expansion. Whereas (β,R) is Borel summable in the PF sector, it becomes Borel nonsummable in the PT sector due to nonlinear terms with (Π¯pt,π¯pt), which is Borel nonsummable. After computation of the PT sector, the NP sectors can be recursively obtained in a similar way. The nth NP sector is labeled by n in the higher transmonomial as e-n·Sw. Although our dynamical system consists of four variables, (β,R,Π¯,π¯), their resurgent relation is the same form derived from the type of ODE as dYdw=-SY+1w[V+BY]+O(Y2,w-2) and contains two Stokes constants, A±. These Stokes constants are functions of (σβ,σR).

sec.p: We have mentioned additional remarks related to transseries structure and resurgent relation in Sec. V. We made comments on the change of transseries and the resurgence in some particular cases such as broken U(1) symmetry, the massless case, and generalized relaxation time in Secs. V A–V C. In addition, we have mentioned the (local forward) attractor solution from the aspect of the IR transseries in Sec. V D. The memory-loss effect of the UV domain characterized by the exponential decay does not appear due to a physical scale such as a particle mass and a chemical potential.

Not only just as a method of approximation, transseries analysis and resurgence theory are powerful mathematical methods to provide rich information about hydrodynamics and the kinetic theoretical approach by looking to their structure. If a local equilibrium is consistently defined, then constructions of IR transmonomials and transseries by labeling “sectors” can be performed consistently with an underlying method for formulating hydrodynamics such as Chapman-Enskog expansion, as we can see in Fig. 4.19
One of the exceptions is Gubser flow. In this model, the shear viscosity does not converges to zero in the IR limit due to the nontrivial background geometry, and the NP sector does not exist. See Ref. [59]. This lesson suggests the large possibility of application of transseries analysis and resurgence theory to a more generic setup of hydrodynamics and kinetic theory motivated by QCD. One of the interesting issues is a relationship between transseries structure and symmetry. In this work, we imposed strong symmetry, i.e., Bjorken symmetry, to the theory, but one can expect that a more interesting feature can be seen by relaxing symmetry, e.g., by introducing magnetic source fields. In such a case, the Boltzmann equation generally becomes PDE, and its transseries structure and resurgent relation must become much more nontrivial. We will study these formal constructions based on resurgence theory as future works.

app.title: TRANSSERIES AND BOREL RESUMMATION
app.p: In this appendix, we summarize topics related to transseries, Borel resummation, and resurgence. In Appendix B 1, we briefly explain construction of the transmonomials, which are ingredients of the full transseries solutions, from the ODEs (20)–(25) in the large w. In Appendix B 2, we summarize explicit forms of the results of the first few orders of other variables such as the energy density and the bulk pressure. We give a brief review of Borel resummation in Appendix B 3 and then derive the resurgent relation in Appendix B 4. See Refs. [6–13,45], for example, in more detail.

sec.title: Construction of transmonomials
sec.p: In this part, we derive transmonomials expanded around w=+∞. We take m=1 for simplicity. Let us start with ODEs given by Eqs. (20)–(23). We first assume that limw→+∞Π¯=limw→+∞π¯=0 and limw→+∞β=+∞. From Eqs. (20) and (21), the leading order of (β,α) is given by dβdw∼2wβ,dRdw∼1wO(β-1)⇒β∼σβw2,R∼σR.(B1)The leading order of (β,R) and Eqs. Review of Borel resummation
sec.p: In this part, we briefly review Borel resummation theory. We suppose the following transseries expanded around w=+∞: X(w)∼∑n∈N0ζnX[n](w),X[n](w)∼∑k∈N0a[n,k]w-k,ζ=σe-Swwb,(B22)where w∈R, a[n,k]∈C, b∈C\Z0-, S∈{x∈C|Rex>0}, σ∈C. In the main text, we call the PT sector for n=0 and the nth NP sector if n≠0. For simplicity, we assume that a[0,0]=0. For the technical reasons, we redefine Eq. (B22) as Xˇ[n](w)=w-nbX[n](w)(B23)such that ζnX[n](w)=(σe-Sw)nXˇ[n](w). The Borel transform, B, to Xˇ[n](w) is defined as X^[n](ξ)≔B[Xˇ[n]](ξ)=∑k∈N0a[n,k]Γ(k+nb)ξk+nb-1(ξ∈C).(B24)To avoid confusion, we also define Iξ≔B[w-1]. It is a homomorphism, and the multiplication of B[X](ξ) and B[Y](ξ) is defined using the convolution * as B[X·Y](ξ)=B[X]*B[Y](ξ)≔∫0ξdξ′B[X](ξ′)B[Y](ξ-ξ′).(B25)The Laplace integral using the integration ray with a complex phase θ, Lθ, is defined as Xˇex,θ[n](w)≔Lθ[X^[n]](w)≔∫0+∞eiθdξe-ξwX^[n](ξ).(B26)In this paper, we consider the case that θ=0 or 0±. Taking the asymptotic limit, |w|→+∞, to Xˇex,0[n](w) reduces to Xˇ[n](w) in Eq. (B23). The combination of the Borel transform and the Laplace integral, Sθ≔Lθ∘B, is called Borel resummation. It is important that the Borel resummation is homomorphism, i.e., Sθ[f·g]=Sθ[f]·Sθ[g].

If Xˇ[n](w) is Borel nonsummable along θ=0, meaning that the Laplace integral is not performable because of singular points on the real positive axis on the Borel plane, we introduce the infinitesimal complex phase, θ=0±, to avoid them in the Laplace integral. In such a case, due to the singular points, the resulting Borel resummed function (or transseries) has discontinuity, S0+[Xˇ[n]](w)≠S0-[Xˇ[n]](w).(B27)Here, we formally introduce the Stokes automorphism, Sθ, to make Eq. (B27) to be equality as S0+[Xˇ[n]](w)=S0-∘S0[Xˇ[n]](w).(B28)If Xˇ[n](w) is Borel summable along θ=0, then S0=id and S0+[Xˇ[n]](w)=S0-[Xˇ[n]](w). From now on, we omit the subscript θ in Sθ because we only consider the case that θ=0. The Stokes automorphism is a mapping from a transseries to a transseries generally including exponential decay. So, it can be extended to group transformation by introducing a real parameter, ν∈R, as S→Sν defined as Sν=exp[ν∑ξ*∈ΓΔ•ξ*],Δ•ξ*≔e-ξ*wΔξ*,(B29)where Γ is a set of singular points on the positive real axis of the Borel plane and Δξ* is the alien derivative with respect to the singular point, ξ*. The alien derivative is a mapping from a formal transseries to the same type of a formal transseries, Δξ*: w-bC[[w-1]]→w-b′C[[w-1]],(B30)with some b′∈C. Notice that Sν=0=id and that S in Eq. (B28) is identical to Sν=1. The transformation of Stokes automorphism depends on a given problem. We construct the resurgent relation, which is a relationship among sectors, by defining the transformation based on the structure of our ODE in the next section.
For the i-dimensional vectorial expression, X=(X1,…,Xi), the above definition is applicable by the extension such as n→n∈Ni,ζn→ζn=∏j=1iζjnj with ζi=σie-Siw/wbi on the real positive axis.

sec.p: In this part, we review the construction of the resurgent relation. In this paper, we only consider the case reproducing the PT sector from the NP sectors, but other cases are also possible. See Refs. [8–12] in detail.

We define X˜≔UX¯, where X˜=(X˜+,X˜-)⊤ and X¯=(Π¯,π¯)⊤, which has the following asymptotic form: X˜±(w)∼∑n∈N02ζnX˜±[n](w),X˜±[n](w)=∑k∈N0aX˜±[n,k]w-k.(B31)Notice that aX˜+[(0,1),0]=aX˜-[(1,0),0]=0. For the simplified notation, we define Xˇ±[n](w)=w-n·ρX˜±[n](w).(B32)

sec.p: We first consider the situation that the noncollision term is dominant in this limit. In this case, the CPs are given by solving the following equations: Π¯UV3+2π¯UV+C0D(Ra)(Π¯UV-π¯UV)Π¯UV=0,(C8)43C0β¯π(Ra)-3821π¯UV+45Π¯UV+C0D(Ra)(Π¯UV-π¯UV)π¯UV=0,(C9)where (Π¯UV,π¯UV)≔lims→+∞(Π¯(s),π¯(s)). Notice that the possibility that Π¯UV=π¯UV=0 is rejected because in this case lims→+∞α(s)=σα and Eq. (C9) does not give Π¯UV=π¯UV=0. In addition, the case that α→-∞ is also rejected because |Ra|→+∞ and (β¯π,D) becomes complex value in this domain. Thus, the allowed situation is only α→+∞ and Ra→0. The real solution in this situation is obtained as (Π¯UV,π¯UV)≈(1.0518,-1.5367).(C10)From Eqs. The solution is given by (Π¯UV,σβ)=(1.0868,0.5640θ0)and(0.24468,-0.4083θ0),(C14)and the integration constant, σβ, cannot be taken freely. The second solution is unphysical because of the negative σβ. The leading orders of α and R are obtained as α∼2logs+σα,R∼σRs-2,(C15)in both of the solutions. Then, we consider the stability around the CPs. It can be obtained from the Jacobian defined as J^UV≔(∂F^Π¯∂Π¯∂F^Π¯∂π¯∂F^π¯∂Π¯∂F^π¯∂π¯)|(Π¯,π¯)→(Π¯UV,π¯UV)·s,(C16)where s in the r.h.s. is the regularization. When using w=1/(sβ) for the flow time, these CPs do not appear because 1-(χβ+Π¯-π¯)→0 and all of Eqs. (20)–(23) are singular in the limit. More precisely, it comes from the fact that τ and w are not one-to-one correspondence.
